# Audience and purpose

## Define a useful audience

Avoid "all users" unless the content truly serves everyone in the same way. Describe the reader by their context and task, not by an invented demographic profile.

Useful audience statement:

> A first-time employee who has been asked to request access and does not know the internal access-management terminology.

Less useful:

> Modern digital users who want seamless access experiences.

## Five-part reader brief

Before writing, define:

| Field | Question |
|---|---|
| Audience | Who is likely to read this? |
| Starting knowledge | What do they already know—and not know? |
| Context | What prompted them to open this page? |
| Task | What are they trying to understand, decide, or do? |
| Outcome | What should they be able to do or explain afterward? |

Then write one primary message:

> If the reader remembers only one thing, it should be: **[message].**

## Jobs-to-be-done lens

Phrase the reader's need as an action:

- "I need to understand whether this tool is relevant to my work."
- "I need to complete the request without guessing."
- "I need to know who owns the next step."
- "I need to explain the change to my team."

This is more actionable than a topic label such as "Access Request Overview."

## Assumptions

If audience information is missing, make the least risky assumption. For broad internal content, default to an intelligent non-specialist who is new to the topic. Do not invent research, personas, pain points, or user quotes. Note assumptions only when they materially affect interpretation or instructions.
